title: In waves
hookLine: grief comes in waves, and research doesn't support neat "stages"

cards: A man is in the cereal aisle, some weeks after his mother's funeral, and he's fine. He's checking prices. Then he sees her brand of tea on the shelf, the one with the yellow box, and he's not fine at all.
He stands there holding a basket, crying, while a stranger reaches politely around him for the oatmeal. By the checkout, he's making small talk with the cashier about the weather.
If grief were a staircase, that aisle would look like falling back to the bottom. It isn't a staircase.

teach.h: THE STAGES BEGAN WITH THE DYING
teach.b: First, where the stages came from.
The psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross spent time with dying patients and, in her book On Death and Dying, described stages she saw in them: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance.
She was writing about people facing their own death. The list traveled, and came to be used as a map for anyone grieving anyone. Second, what research on grieving people has found.
Researchers have not found that grief moves through fixed stages in a set order. People differ, and one person can feel several things in an afternoon.
Kübler-Ross herself later said the stages were never meant as a tidy sequence. Third, a better picture.

teach.h: TOWARD THE LOSS, THEN BACK TO LIFE
teach.b: The grief researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut describe grieving people moving back and forth: toward the loss, with its memories and tears, then toward ordinary life, cooking, paying the bills, laughing at something on television, then back again.
They call it oscillation. In their model, the swing isn't a failure to grieve properly. It's how people cope.
Fourth, an older poet found the same image.
In Psalm 42, a singer far from home says: "Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me."
Waves rise, break over you, and pull back. Over time they can come further apart, though a big one can still arrive on an ordinary Tuesday, in a grocery aisle. Not stages.

how: Grief counselors who work with the dual process model encourage people to let themselves turn toward the loss and then back to daily life, without treating the swing between them as going backward.

o: grief climbing through five fixed stages to the end
grief that fades steadily a little more every day
grief rising and falling, toward the loss and back to life

games.q: who described what — tap the pairs.
p: all thy waves and thy billows
a wave on an ordinary day

s: Kübler-Ross first described her stages in people facing their own death
On Death and Dying was about dying patients, not mourners.
research shows grief moves through fixed stages in order
researchers have not found a set order; people differ.
turning back to ordinary life means you're not grieving properly
in Stroebe and Schut's model, the swing is how people cope.

games.q: you're in the grocery store, weeks after a funeral, and a wave hits at the shelf. what do you do?
o: decide you've slid back to the first stage.
let it come and pass, then finish your shopping.
leave, and never shop there again.
games.why: waves rise and pull back; turning back to ordinary life afterward is part of grieving, not a step backward.

practice: Bring to mind a loss you can hold safely right now, a move, an ending, a friendship that faded, and if a large one feels too much today, choose a small one.
Let the feeling rise a little, notice where it sits, the throat, the chest, behind the eyes, and breathe without pushing it down or stirring it up.
Then gently turn toward something ordinary, the weight of the chair, your feet on the floor; that turning is part of grieving too.

wordCard.voice: In waves: grief rising and falling, toward the loss and back to life, rather than climbing a staircase of stages. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: deep calleth unto deep. A wave can come, and pass. Day seven hundred ninety-nine, done.
